IFD0:XPSubject: This photograph captures the interior of the historic Church of Saint-Antoine-de-Padoue in Batoche, Saskatchewan. During the North-West Rebellion (or North-West Resistance) of 1885, the church and its adjacent rectory served a pivotal role. The Métis leader Louis Riel used the building as his headquarters, and it was also used as a hospital and a defensive position during the Battle of Batoche. This specific image shows how the interior looked roughly 40 years after those events, around 1926.

IFD0:XPSubject: The homes of Rooster Town were constructed almost entirely of found materials in the surrounding areas. The Canadian National Railways unknowingly provided most of the building materials for the homes. The railways Harte subdivision stored boxcars in off season, and their wooden partitions provided ideal home building material.[22] It is evident in this image that the siding is from CN boxcars. Also, this image shows the close kinship ties within Rooster Town. In many cases, several generations lived together in one home. This is similar to how their ancestors lived before colonization. Image From: PC18/5874/18-5874-003, Winnipeg Tribune Collection, Department of Archives and Special Collections, Elizabeth Dafoe Library, University of Manitoba.
_drive_description:
CREDIT: University of Manitoba Archives & Special Collections, 
Winnipeg Tribune fonds

December 20, 1951

The Cardinal boys, seven-year-old Ronnie and five-year-old Frank, get ready to leave their Rooster Town shack and hike three-quarters of a mile for a can of water. Mrs. Archie Cardinal stands talking to them and their two-year-old brother is seen peering out the shack door.
